If we were replacing computers, then AI is great. The issue is that searching through documents, spelling, math, grammar, memorization, training, and knowledge are all learned through study and repetition. If we have a computer doing all that work, then people stop being designers, engineers, writers, teachers, or workers, and instead start becoming nothing but decision makers. When the hardest part of your job is making decisons, what would you say the next automation will be? The census data is promising when applied to robotics or CAD, but it doesn't solve the problem that comes about when you factor in learning. People know what to ask AI because they learned a whole lot more than what one question. The automatic elevator didn't take away the need for basic reasoning in a job. AI is demolishing paralegal, 2 year architecture, and entry level engineering jobs. It's too early to tell with any real certainty what the impact of AI will be. We know that robotics and automation made things more efficient with only some degree of damage to the performance of most humans, but we don't know the degree to which AI will impact nit just human ability, but the human experience. If you aren't alive to work for youself or others, then what is the point?

European here. Let face it. Salaries in US (or San Francisco ?) are crazy. I saw some charts that some L3 (regular ?) hires have around 300k $ in FAANG companies. Now, let me tell you that in Poland, in Warsaw (capital city), most probably you'll get equal engineer for like 5, 6, 7k $ a month = 60-70k $ yearly. So, for one US L3 engineer, you can get something like 4, 5, 6 engineers speaking fluently in English, very well educated, living in super modern city, knowing all trends, bells and whistles. What if you outsource to India ? Well, I don't know the salaries in India, but I can assume that is probably 2, 3, 4 (?) times lower than in Poland, so all in all it translates that for one normal (I mean L3 is nothing extraodrinary - there are thousands engineers like this in every bigger country) US engineer you can get most probably whole team of 7, 8, 10 (?) engineers in India. ps. I disagree that FAANG is a holy grail. I don't know, maybe in US. Me, as software engineer, I want to create new things, innovative, or at least have some kind of a impact (so smaller startup, project that will help my customer / real people) - so let's say that there is some company with real, physical product but their IT is outdated -> then it is exciting to bring them back into XXI century, clouds etc. (even if technically at Google it is on far, far better level).. Google, Meta ? Seriously, what did they create in last 10, 15 years ? Nothing. Pure nothing. They're no longer tech-companies to be honest. They only maintaint the products they created 10, 15 years ago and they squeeze them to the limit. That's why there are the layoffs. Every year, board needs numbers. It's the easiest way to get numbers - fire people. Also, it's actually pretty scary - Microsoft has like 200k employees ? That's crazy. Such compoanies are super, duper ineffective and that's why in last 10, 15 years they werent able to innovate anything. It's funny that company out of nowhere Open AI created a product everybody talks about (Chat GPT), everybody uses. So, in 5-7 years, they took the lead, almost without these big behemot corporations reaction. What did Meta do ? Nothing. They're just moving buttons on facebook app, or instagram, or whatever. What did Amazon do ? At least they maintain AWS ;) Google ? Yeah, month by month they're making Google Search less useful and throw AI just like "HD Ready" or "gluten free" slogans ;p How many engineers are hired there ? Is it 80 % ? I bet, half of the people are soft, "management" roles, while in reality these people are just taking salaries. If I would become a CEO of Google or Meta or Microsoft, I would fire like half of the people - leaving only engineers and super small amount of management roles (just like Elon, to be honest). Then you can innovate. The question, of course is - do they want to innovate ? I don't think so. Like you said, these companies are no longer tech-companies... They don't improve tech at all. They're stagnant for years. ps. when I got my first IT job (Java Developer) in 2005, I didn't know to be honest what will be my salary. I liked programming, was passionate about it, was passionate about the freedom it gives you to build things. NOW, or lets say in last 10 years - thousands or millions of people (who should never get into IT) got into IT mainly for $$$ reasons and it got corrupted like a cancer to be honest. More and more people have no clue about engineering job at these companies. There just bunch of fake roles, management knowing nothing about IT and thinking it's ok ("i'm not technical" - well, then leave IT), idiotic "day of life as a software engineer" girls to maybe should simply create OF accounts instead ;p
